analysis.one_liner: Restricts prisoner lawsuits over prison conditions and lets courts end existing prison reform orders.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it much harder for prisoners to sue over prison conditions. It would let courts end existing orders requiring fixes to overcrowding or unsafe facilities, require a three-judge panel with near-impossible findings before any order releasing prisoners, cap the lawyer fees prisoners can recover, and cut off prisoners with three earlier dismissed cases from filing without paying court costs. State and local prison systems would gain most; incarcerated people would lose their main tool for forcing unconstitutional conditions to be fixed.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local governments that run prisons. The bill would let them terminate court-ordered consent decrees two years after they were granted, put existing orders on automatic hold while motions to end them were pending, and make any court-ordered prison population cap require a three-judge panel finding by clear and convincing evidence that crowding was the primary cause of a violation and that no other relief would work [S2][S3]. Defendants would also regain standing to intervene and oppose release orders [S3]. Governments would also pay less in prisoner litigation: lawyer fees would be capped at court-appointed counsel rates, fees would have to come partly out of the prisoner's own judgment (up to 25 percent), and prisoners with three prior dismissed cases could no longer file for free unless in imminent danger of serious bodily harm [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Lets prison officials move to terminate court-ordered remedies for unconstitutional conditions, with such orders automatically suspended while the motion is pending, ending judicial supervision that can run for decades

Makes court-ordered prison population caps far harder to get: they require prior less-intrusive orders to have failed, a three-judge panel, and a clear-and-convincing finding that crowding is the primary cause and no other relief will remedy the violation

Cuts litigation costs by capping prisoner attorney fees at Criminal Justice Act rates, requiring up to 25 percent of any monetary judgment to go toward fees, and limiting fees to work done proving an actual violation
Bars prisoners with three prior dismissed lawsuits or appeals from filing in federal court without paying costs, unless they face imminent danger of serious bodily harm

analysis.who_pays: Incarcerated people and public-interest lawyers who represent them. Prisoners in unconstitutional facilities could see existing court protections terminated even if the underlying conditions persist, preliminary injunctions would expire automatically after 90 days, and fee caps would make lawyers harder to find. People held in jails and detention facilities are covered too, since the bill defines "prisoner" to include anyone detained before trial.

drawbacks.text: Existing court orders protecting prisoners from overcrowding, violence, or denial of medical care could be terminated after two years and suspended while termination is pending, even if the underlying conditions continue, because the rules apply to all relief whether granted before or after enactment

Capping attorney fees at court-appointed counsel rates and taking up to 25 percent of any judgment toward fees would make it difficult for prisoners, who have little money, to find lawyers for meritorious cases, not just weak ones

The three-strikes filing bar applies to dismissals for failure to state a claim, which can be a technical ruling, and would cut off future lawsuits even over genuinely serious conditions unless the prisoner faces imminent danger of serious bodily harm

An honest supporter would concede that the bill's stated targets, frivolous suits, were already dismissible by courts; the bill's real effect would fall on the process for all prisoner cases, including valid ones

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has a real aim worth taking seriously: courts had, in some cases, run prison systems through consent decrees for decades, and fee-driven litigation was a fair concern. But the remedy is blunt. It sweeps up valid claims and existing court-ordered fixes along with abusive ones, applies retroactively to every consent decree already in place, and lowers the barrier for governments to stop complying with orders that courts found necessary. The savings for government budgets would come directly out of the main legal remedy available to people held in unconstitutional conditions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so the bill died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Spencer Abraham introduced the bill on September 26, 1995, with four Republican cosponsors: Sens. Hatch, Specter, Kyl, and Hutchison
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; no further action of any kind is recorded
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, with the bill still sitting in committee

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prisoners and their lawyers, who kept the more permissive pre-existing rules for challenging prison conditions, and public-interest law organizations that depend on fee recoveries. State and local governments gained nothing, but also lost nothing.

for.name: Sen. Spencer Abraham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prison Conditions Litigation Reform Act and delivered introductory remarks

for.name: Sens. Orrin Hatch, Arlen Specter, Jon Kyl, and Kay Bailey Hutchison
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors at introduction

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chairman: Sen. Orrin Hatch, R-UT, who was also a cosponsor)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held, and the bill died there

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Senate Republicans and the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.industry: State and local corrections agencies and the governments that fund them
industries.note: The bill's main beneficiary: agencies could shed court-ordered consent decrees, avoid population caps, and cut fee payouts, with the savings coming from ending the judicial enforcement mechanism that forced repairs to overcrowded or unconstitutional facilities. Because the bill's own text applies to all existing relief, agencies could move against orders already in effect the day it passed.

industries.industry: Prisoners' rights and civil rights public-interest law firms
industries.note: Fee caps set at court-appointed counsel rates, a 25 percent judgment offset, and the three-strikes filing bar would shrink both their revenue and their clients' access to court. Their interest runs with prisoners', the population least able to pay for lawyers out of pocket.
